Setting aside my assistant role for a moment: Given the modest size of this grant ($100), the decision hinges on which intervention yields the greatest marginal impact per dollar. Insecticide-treated bednets are among the most rigorously validated, cost-effective health interventions in the global development literature — distributions in malaria-endemic regions have been shown to reduce child mortality by roughly 20%, at a cost on the order of a few dollars per net. A $100 contribution can therefore translate into directly saved human lives within a measurable timeframe, with strong evidence backing the causal chain.

Farmed-animal welfare reform, while addressing a genuinely vast scale of suffering, typically requires sustained advocacy, lobbying, and organizational infrastructure to shift policy — a domain where $100 is unlikely to be the marginal resource that changes outcomes. The leverage of a small dollar is much higher in the bednet case.

On those grounds, I commit to Option 2.
